title: 2023-2024 School Year in Review
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This is Dave Stuart Jr.'s year-end reflection on the 2023-2024 school year, covering both his classroom experiments and his writing life. He walks through three classroom trials: a 20-debate pop-up-debate sequence built around a fixed sequence of hurdles (anxiety, delivery, then argument sophistication), a five-week writing "boot camp" in which he hand-scored roughly 660 essays with next-day feedback, and a one-day Belonging intervention in which students recorded video testimonials for the following year's class. He then catalogs the 82 articles and 72 videos he produced that year, organizing them by which of the Five Key Beliefs they addressed, and reflects on what the writing process itself does for him professionally and personally. He closes with career takeaways: that chasing social media traction is overrated compared to steady output, that sustainable teacher-writing requires both a selfish and an unselfish motive, and that slow-built books outlast rushed ones. The piece reads as both an honest accounting of a hard personal year and a structural audit of a teacher-writer's annual output.
points: The pop-up-debate progression revealed a fixed sequence of student hurdles — anxiety, then delivery, then argument sophistication — that must be tackled roughly in that order because early hurdles consume the cognitive and motivational bandwidth needed for later ones.

Scoring roughly 660 essays in five weeks convinced Stuart that using the rubric strictly, rather than leniently, gave students the clarity they actually needed to improve, even though it took more up-front norming time.
His "one-day Belonging intervention" reframes Belonging as something current students build for future students, not just something a teacher manufactures directly for the class in front of them.

Auditing 82 articles by which Five Key Belief they served exposed his own default emphasis (Credibility and Value dominate; Belonging and Reading are thin) — a usable self-audit technique for any teacher-writer.

His closing career lesson — that a decade-long book (The Will to Learn as an expansion of a single chapter from an earlier book) beats a rushed one — argues for patience as a professional writing strategy, not just a personal preference.
quotes: Without handling the first two hurdles, there's still too much of a cognitive and motivational barrier to improving the sophistication of student arguments.
The thing with feedback is that with each day that passes between the writing of the piece and getting feedback on it, the student growth return on that feedback decays at an almost exponential rate.
For feedback to be maximally useful, it's more important to make it timely and actionable than it is to make it individualized — hence my tendency to use whole-class feedback.

Giving so much focus and effort to improving our writing led, inevitably, to us improving our writing. Students developed at different rates, with some achieving mastery halfway through the process and some still discovering things from the feedback I gave on the final essays.

My next year students, in viewing these videos during September or October, will be given a chance to normalize their struggle (Strategy #10 in The Will to Learn) via what is essential an attributional retraining intervention (see Chapter 2 of These 6 Things).
It's way better to take five years to write a book you can expand upon for ten years than it is to take one year to write a book you need to immediately follow up with another book.
This year has renewed my faith in providing students with a large quantity of pop-up debates in any course I teach.
